title: Google Meet AI Notes and To-Dos, Automatically
title_options: Google Meet AI Notes and To-Dos, Automatically
Auto Meeting Notes in Google Meet (Otter or Fireflies)
Turn Any Meeting Into Notes and To-Dos Automatically
description_intro: Set up a free AI note-taker like Otter.ai or Fireflies for Google Meet, so every call ends with a transcript, a summary and action items. Then turn that summary into a to-do table and a follow-up email with ChatGPT; every prompt is below.
prompts_used: Invite line: An AI note-taker will join to record and summarise this call. Tell me before we start if you'd rather it didn't.
Turn these meeting notes into a table with three columns: task, owner, deadline. Flag any task that has no owner or no deadline. [paste summary]
Write a short follow-up email to the meeting attendees with the decisions we made and this to-do table. Keep it under 150 words. [paste notes and table]
Here are last week's to-dos and today's meeting notes. Which tasks are done, which are late, and which were not mentioned? [paste both]
Say in the meeting: Action item: [name] [does task] by [day].

scenes.voiceover: You leave a one-hour meeting and have to write the notes, the decisions, and who does what. What if that was already in your inbox when the call ended? In this video I'll set up an AI note-taker for Google Meet, step by step, and then turn its summary into a clean to-do list with owners and deadlines. Every prompt is in the description.

You need three things. A Google account with Google Calendar, an AI note-taker like Otter dot A I or Fireflies, and ChatGPT for the final clean-up. Otter and Fireflies both have free plans with limits, so you can test this today without paying anything.

card.heading: What you need
lines: Otter.ai or Fireflies (free plan to start)

scenes.voiceover: Here's how it works. The note-taker joins your Google Meet call as an extra participant, records and transcribes the conversation, then writes a summary with action items. You don't have to press anything during the meeting. You just talk, and the notes arrive afterwards.

card.heading: How it works
lines: 3. You get a summary and to-dos

scenes.voiceover: Why bother? Because taking notes while you talk means you only half listen. And writing them up afterwards eats another twenty or thirty minutes per meeting. If you have five meetings a week, that's two hours or more, every week, spent typing up things people already said out loud.

Step one. Pick one tool and sign up. If your team mostly wants clear summaries and a searchable record, either tool works. Don't sign up for both, or two bots will join every meeting. Sign up with the same Google account your work calendar uses. That makes the next step one click.

card.heading: Step 1: Pick one tool
lines: Sign up with your work Google account

scenes.voiceover: Step two. Connect your Google Calendar. During setup, the tool asks for permission to see your calendar. This is how it knows when your meetings are and which ones have a Google Meet link. Read the permission screen before you accept, so you know what you're sharing.

card.heading: Step 2: Connect your calendar
lines: It finds meetings with a Meet link

scenes.voiceover: Step three. Choose which meetings it joins. Look in the tool's settings for auto-join. Most people start with only meetings they organise, rather than every meeting on the calendar. You can also add it to one meeting at a time, by pasting the Meet link into the tool. Start small, and widen it once you trust the results.

card.heading: Step 3: Set auto-join
lines: Or paste one Meet link manually

scenes.voiceover: Step four. Tell people before it records. The note-taker shows up in the participant list with its own name, but don't rely on that. Add a line to the meeting invite, and say it out loud at the start. Recording rules differ between countries and companies, so getting agreement first protects you and keeps trust in the team. There's a one-line note you can paste into your invite in the description.

card.heading: Step 4: Tell everyone first
lines: Add a line to the invite
Say it at the start of the call

scenes.voiceover: Step five. Have the meeting, then open the notes. Shortly after the call ends, the tool usually emails you a summary, and the full transcript waits in your account. You get an overview, the main topics, and a list of action items, plus a transcript you can search by word.

Spend one minute reading the summary before you do anything else. Check that the main decision is there and that the action items match what you remember. If something's missing, search the transcript for a keyword, find the moment, and copy the exact words into your notes.

card.heading: Read it for one minute
lines: Do the to-dos match your memory?

scenes.voiceover: Step six. Turn the summary into a real to-do list. AI summaries are good, but action items are often vague, like someone will look into it. Copy the summary into ChatGPT with this prompt. Ask for a table with the task, the owner, and the deadline, and ask it to flag anything without an owner.

card.heading: Step 6: Make a to-do list
lines: You: Turn these notes into a table: task, owner, deadline. Flag tasks with no owner.
AI: Send budget draft | Sam | Friday...

scenes.voiceover: Now you can see the gaps at a glance. Any task with no owner or no date is a task that won't happen. Fix those now, while everyone still remembers the meeting, not a week later when nobody does.

Then send the follow-up in one more prompt. Ask ChatGPT to write a short email with the decisions and the to-do table, under one hundred and fifty words. Read it, fix any names, and send it to everyone who was on the call. The whole thing takes about two minutes.

card.heading: The follow-up email
lines: You: Write a short follow-up email with the decisions and this to-do table. Under 150 words.
AI: Hi all, thanks for today. Decisions...

scenes.voiceover: A quick tip for recurring meetings, like a weekly team catch-up. Keep the to-do tables from each week in one document. At the start of the next meeting, paste last week's table into ChatGPT with the new notes, and ask which tasks are done, which are late, and which nobody mentioned. It's a two-minute progress check.

card.heading: Track weekly meetings
lines: You: Here are last week's to-dos and today's notes. Which are done, late, or not mentioned?
AI: Done: budget draft. Late: client deck...

scenes.voiceover: Now three tips. Tip one: say action items out loud, clearly. Something like: action item, Sam sends the report by Friday. When a task is spoken with a name and a day, the AI picks it up far more reliably than a vague maybe.

card.heading: Tip 1: Say it out loud
lines: "Action item: Sam sends the report by Friday"

scenes.voiceover: Tip two: search your old meetings instead of asking around. Because every call is transcribed, you can search a word like budget or launch date and jump straight to the moment it was discussed. Both tools also offer AI chat that answers questions about your meetings, depending on your plan.

card.heading: Tip 2: Search past meetings
lines: AI chat depends on your plan

scenes.voiceover: Tip three: if your company pays for Google Workspace, check whether Google Meet already has a built-in option called take notes for me. It's powered by Gemini and saves notes to Google Docs. It's only on some plans, but if you have it, you may not need a separate tool at all.

card.heading: Tip 3: Check Google Meet first
lines: Uses Gemini, saves to Google Docs

scenes.voiceover: One honest warning. Transcripts are good, not perfect. Names, numbers, and accents trip them up, and the summary can miss a decision or invent a clean ending to a messy discussion. Skim the summary against your own memory before you send it on, and never paste confidential notes into a personal AI account.

card.heading: Check before you share
lines: Names and numbers can be wrong
No confidential notes in personal AI

scenes.voiceover: Also watch the free plan limits. Free plans cap things like the number of minutes, the length of each meeting, or how many transcripts you keep. Use the free plan for a couple of weeks, see how many meetings you really record, and only upgrade if the limits get in your way.

That's the system. Pick one note-taker, connect your calendar, choose which meetings it joins, tell people, then turn the summary into a to-do list and a follow-up email. Next week, making a full presentation in five minutes with AI. Subscribe so you don't miss it.

shorts.title: Say This in Meetings So AI Catches It
shorts.hook: Say this one sentence and your AI note-taker never misses a task.

scenes.voiceover: AI note-takers miss tasks when people say vague things like maybe we should.

card.heading: Vague = missed
lines: AI can't tell who or when

scenes.voiceover: Instead say: action item, Sam sends the report by Friday. A name, a task, and a day.

card.heading: Say it like this
lines: Action item: Sam sends the report by Friday

scenes.voiceover: The AI picks it up, and so does everyone in the room. Follow for more.

shorts.description: One simple habit that makes AI meeting assistants like Otter and Fireflies catch every action item.

fact_check: Otter.ai and Fireflies both have a free plan (with limits on minutes/meeting length/storage) as of today
Both tools can connect to Google Calendar and auto-join Google Meet calls as a visible participant bot
Both tools let you choose auto-join scope (e.g. all meetings vs only meetings you organise) and add a bot to a single meeting by pasting a Meet link
Both tools send/produce a post-meeting summary with action items and a searchable transcript (email delivery may depend on settings)
Both tools offer an AI chat that answers questions about past meetings; the video says 'depending on your plan'
Google Meet 'Take notes for me' (Gemini) exists, saves notes to Google Docs, and is limited to some Workspace plans
Recording-consent wording is general advice, not legal advice; video tells viewers to check company rules
